body.translated_text: For another reason operating in an already-established domain is virtually a synonym — because there is no distinction in what is to be established.

body.text: arthaḥ punaḥ pratipādanānna bhidyate /
body.translated_text: Meaning, moreover, does not differ by [mere] expression.

body.text:
74. yatpunaruktam- "anuvāde tvapunaruktaṃ; śabdābhyāsādarthaviśeṣopapatteḥ" / yathā "hetvapadeśāt pratijñāyāḥ punarvacanaṃ nigamanam" [nya. sū. 1.1.39] iti / pratijñāyā evaṃ [eva?] gamyamānārthāyā vacanaṃ punarvacanaṃ. kiṃ punarasyāḥ punarvacanam ityuyuktaṃ nigamanam /
75. [14.] "vijñātasya parṣadā trirabhihitasyāpratyuccāraṇamananubhāṣaṇam /" [nyā.sū. 5.2.17] vijñātavākyārthasya parṣadā trirabhihitasya yadapratyuccāraṇaṃ tadananubhāṣaṇaṃ nāma nigrahasthānamapratyuccārayan kimāśrayaṃ parapakṣapratiṣedha kuryāditi /
body.translated_text:
74. As for the statement: 'In recapitulation, however, there is no repetition, because a specification of meaning is established from the repetition of words.' For example: 'The restatement of the thesis after the statement of the reason is the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>)' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 1.1.39]. The statement of the thesis, whose meaning is already understood, is a restatement. But what is the purpose of this restatement? It is said to be the conclusion.
75. [14.] 'Non-repetition (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>) is the failure to repeat, after it has been stated thrice, what has been understood by the assembly' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.17]. When one whose statement-meaning has been understood by the assembly, after having been stated thrice, does not repeat it — this so-called 'non-repetition' is a ground for defeat. [The question is:] on what basis would one who does not repeat refute the opponent's thesis?

body.text: uttareṇāvasānānnedaṃ nigrahasthānamiti cet / syādetat / uttareṇa guṇadoṣavatā mūḍhāmūḍhatvaṃ gamyate iti kimuccāritena? asti hi kaścid uttareṇa samartho na pratyuccāraṇena, nāsau tāvatā nigrahamarhediti / na: uttaraviṣayāparijñānāt / yadyayaṃ na pratyuccārayati, nirviṣayamuttaraṃ prasajyeta / athottaraṃ bravīti, kathaṃ noccārayati? tadidaṃ vyāhatamucyate- 'noccārayati, uttaraṃ ca bravīti'; iti / apratijñānācca / na cedaṃ na [? na cedaṃ] parijñāyate- pūrvaṃ sarvamuccārayitavyaṃ paścāduttaramabhidhātavyamiti / apitu yathākathañciduttaraṃ vācyam uttaraṃ cāśrayābhāve 'yuktamiti yuktamapratyuccāraṇaṃ nigrahasthānamiti /
body.translated_text: If [one says:] 'This is not a ground for defeat, because it terminates with the reply' — this might be so. [But:] since the quality or fault of the reply reveals whether one is confused or not, what need is there for repetition? For there is someone who is capable of replying but not of repeating — and that person should not be defeated merely on that account. No — because of failure to ascertain the subject of the reply. If he does not repeat, the reply would be without a subject. But if he does give a reply, how has he not repeated? This then is contradictory — 'he does not repeat, yet he gives a reply.' Also, because there is no convention that everything must first be repeated and only then the reply given. Rather, a reply must be given somehow or other; and since a reply without a basis is improper, it is proper that non-repetition is a ground for defeat.

body.text: 76. yadi nāma vādī svas ādhanārthavivaraṇavyājena prasaṅgādaparaṃ ghoṣayed, vivādāspadaṃ ca jijñāsitamarthamātramukttvā pratijñādiṣvarthaviśeṣaparamparayā aparānarthānupakṣipya kathāṃ vistārayet, tacca sarvaṃ yadā nānuvaktuṃ śaknuyāt, kastasya vivādāśrayārthamātrottaravacane sāmarthyavighātaḥ yena vādivacanānubhāṣaṇaṃ nigrahasthānamucyate / tasmānna sarvaṃ vādikathāmananubhāṣamāṇo nottare samarthaḥ /
body.translated_text: 76. If the proponent, under the pretext of elaborating on the meaning of his proof, should by digressions make the other [respondent] shout [in confusion], and having stated merely the matter under dispute, should extend the discourse by introducing a series of other irrelevant details in the thesis and so forth — and when [the respondent] is unable to repeat all of that, what impediment is there to his ability to reply on just the subject-matter of the dispute? — by which the non-repetition of the proponent's statement is called a ground for defeat. Therefore, one who does not repeat all of the proponent's discourse is not thereby incapable of replying.

body.text: yadvacanāntarīyakā jijñāsitārthasiddhiḥ, yathā pakṣadharmatāvyāptiprasādhanamātraṃ, na tatrāpi prasaṅgāntaropakṣepaḥ, tadavaśyaṃ sādhanāṅgaviṣayatvād dūṣaṇasya upadarśyata eva / tatrāpi na sarvaṃ prāganukrameṇoccārayitavyaṃ, paścād dūṣaṇaṃ vācyaṃ; dviruccāraṇaprasaṅgāt / dūṣaṇaviṣayopadarśanārthe 'nubhāṣaṇe vādivacanānukramaghoṣaṇaṃ vyarthamiti na kāryameva dūṣayatā / 'asyāyaṃ doṣoḥ'; iti nāntarīyatvāt pratidoṣavacanaṃ viṣayopadarśanaṃ kriyate eva /
body.translated_text: That upon whose utterance the establishment of the matter under investigation depends — such as merely the establishment of the thesis-property and pervasion — there too no extraneous <s>prasaṅga</s> should be introduced, because the refutation necessarily pertains to a component of the proof and is therefore demonstrated. There too, one need not first repeat everything in order and then state the refutation — for that would entail double utterance. In repetition for the purpose of showing the subject of refutation, the sequential recitation of the proponent's words is pointless and need not be done by the refuter. 'This is the fault of this' — because it necessarily involves showing the subject of refutation with each fault-statement.

body.text: 77. na hi sarvaviṣayopadarśanaṃ kṛtvā yugapad doṣaḥ śakyate 'bhidhātum; pratyarthaṃ doṣabhedāt / tasmād yaṃ padārthaṃ dūṣayati, sa eva taddūṣaṇaviṣayastadā pradarśanīyaḥ / (

children.text: ) nāparastuḥ; dūṣṇe 'paropadarśanasyāsambhavāt / tasmin dūṣite punaranyo 'rtho 'paradoṣaviṣaya ityayamanubhāṣaṇe dūṣaṇe ca nyāyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Not the other — because the indication of the other is impossible during [the current] refutation. When that [first topic] has been refuted, then the next topic becomes the subject of the next fault — this is the proper method of repetition and refutation.

body.translated_text: 77. For it is not possible to show all subjects and then state all faults simultaneously, because the faults differ for each topic. Therefore, whichever topic one refutes, that alone should be indicated at that time as the subject of that refutation.

body.text: sakṛt sarvānubhāṣaṇe 'pi doṣavacanakāle punarviṣayaḥ pradarśanīya eva; apradarśite doṣasya vaktumaśakyatvāt / tathā ca dviranubhāṣaṇaṃ kṛtaṃ syāt / tatra prathamaṃ sarvānukramānubhāṣaṇaṃ niṣprayojanam / dūṣaṇavādinā dūṣaṇe vaktavye yanna tatropayujyate tasyābhidānamadoṣodbhāvanam / dviruktiśca / iti sakṛt sarvānubhāṣaṇaṃ parājayādhikaraṇaṃ vācyam /
body.translated_text: Even if one repeats everything at once, at the time of stating faults one must indicate the subject again — because without indication the fault cannot be stated. And so, repetition would be done twice. In that case, the first complete sequential repetition is purposeless. For the refuter, when stating the refutation, the utterance of what is not useful for that purpose constitutes 'non-raising of a fault.' And there is double utterance. Therefore, complete one-time repetition should be called a ground for defeat.

body.text: tathāstviti cet / syādetat / uktametadarthāntaraṃ nigrahasthānamiti / tatra sādhane yataḥ kutaścit prasaṅgādinā nāntarīyakābhidhāna / ['nāntarīyakābhidhānaṃ?] vādino 'rthāntaragamanameveti sa nigrahārhaḥ / na kaścit kvacit kriyamāṇaprasaṅgo na prayujyate, nāpi tat tasyānubhāṣaṇīyam / na cedamapyasmābhiranujñāyate- sarvaṃ prāk sakṛdvaktavyaṃ, paścāddūṣaṇamiti / kintu dūṣayatāvaśyaṃ viṣayo darśanīyaḥ, anyathā dūṣaṇāvṛtteriti /
body.translated_text: If [one says:] 'Let it be so' — it may be said that this has been stated [already as] 'departure to another topic is a ground for defeat.' There, in the proof, non-essential utterance from some <s>prasaṅga</s> or the like constitutes the proponent's departure to another topic, and he deserves defeat. No <s>prasaṅga</s> being introduced anywhere is ever useful, nor should it be repeated. Nor do we approve of this — that everything must first be said once and then the refutation [given]. Rather, the refuter must show the subject — otherwise, the refutation would be incomplete.

body.text: 78. evaṃ tarhi nānanubhāṣaṇaṃ pṛthag nigrahasthānaṃ vācyam, apratibhayā gatatvāt / uttarasya hyapratipattirapratibhā [nyā.sū. 5.2.18] / na cottaraviṣayamapradarśayan uttaraṃ pratipattuṃ sararthaḥ / na hyanākṣiptānuttarapratipattikamananubhāṣaṇam / tenānanubhāṣaṇasya vyāpikāyāmapratibhāyāṃ vihitaṃ nigrahasthānatvam ananubhāṣaṇam [ananubhāṣaṇe?] / gavyaparāmṛṣṭatadbhedāyāṃ vihitamiva sāsnādimattvaṃ bāhuleye 'pi / tasmādpratibhaiva nigrahādhikaraṇatvena vā [vācyā?] nānanubhāṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: 78. If so, then non-repetition (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>) need not be stated separately as a ground for defeat, because it is already covered by 'failure to respond' (<s>apratibhā</s>). For the failure to comprehend a reply is [precisely] 'failure to respond' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.18]. And one who does not show the subject of the reply cannot comprehend the reply. For non-repetition that does not elicit a basis for reply [is not truly non-repetition]. Therefore, since 'failure to respond' pervades non-repetition, the ground-for-defeat status prescribed for non-repetition [is redundant] — like prescribing 'having a dewlap' for <s>bāhuleya</s> (a breed of cattle) when it has already been prescribed for the class 'bovine' of which [bāhuleya] is a sub-type. Therefore, either 'failure to respond' alone should be stated as the ground for defeat, or non-repetition [should not be stated separately].

body.text: kaścāyaṃsamayaniyamastrirabhihitasyānanubhāṣaṇamiti? yadi tāvat parapratyāyanārthā pravṛttiḥ, kiṃ trirabhidhīyeta? tathā tathā sa grāhaṇīyo yathāsya pratipattirbhavati / atha paropatāpanārthā tadāpi kiṃ trirabhidhīyate? sākṣiṇāṃ karṇe nivedya prativādī kaṣṭāpratītadrutasaṃkṣisādibhirupadrotavyaḥ, yathottarapratipattivimūḍhastūṣṇīmbhavati / na hi paropatāpanakrame kaścinnyāyaḥ, yena kaṣṭāpratītaprayogadrutoccāritā nivāryante, trirabhidhānaṃ vā vidhīyate / na ca paropatāpāya santaḥ pravartante, śāstrāṇi vā praṇīyante ityado vakttavyam ! tasmāttāvadvaktavyaṃ, yāvadanena na gṛhītam / na trireva /
body.translated_text: And what is this conventional rule 'non-repetition of what has been stated thrice'? If the activity is for the purpose of convincing the other, why should [something] be stated [only] thrice? It should be repeated in whatever way produces understanding in the other. If the activity is for the purpose of harassing the other, then again why only thrice? One should inform the witnesses and then harass the respondent with utterances that are hard to understand, rapid, compressed, and so forth, so that he becomes confused about replying and falls silent. For in the procedure of harassing others, there is no rule by which hard-to-understand constructions and rapid utterances are prohibited, or thrice-stating is prescribed. And since the virtuous do not engage in harassing others, nor are treatises composed for that purpose — this is what should be said! Therefore, one should speak as many times as needed until the other has understood — not just thrice.

body.text: agrahaṇasāmarthye prāgeva vā paricchinnasāmarthye parihartavyaḥ punaranupratibodhyeti /
body.translated_text: If [the respondent] lacks the ability to understand, or if his ability has already been determined [to be insufficient], he should be dismissed and re-instructed [later].

body.text: 79. [15.] "avijñātamajñānam /" [nyā.sū. 5.2.17] vijñātaṃ parṣadā prativādinā yadavijñātaṃ tadajñānaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam / arthe khalvavijñāte na tasya pratiṣedhaṃ brūyāditi /
body.translated_text: 79. [15.] 'What is not understood is ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>)' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.17]. That which is understood by the assembly but not understood by the respondent — that so-called 'ignorance' is a ground for defeat. [The idea is:] when the meaning is not understood, one cannot state its refutation.

body.text: etadapyananubhāṣaṇavadatreti tatraiva gamyatvādavācyam / yathānanubhāṣaṇe 'pradarśitaviṣayatvāduttarapratipattiraśakyeti anuttarapratipattyaiva nigrahasthānatvam; uttaraviṣayapradarśanaprasaṅgamantareṇānubhāṣaṇasya vaiyarthyāt /
body.translated_text: This too, like non-repetition, need not be stated separately, since it is already covered thereby. Just as in non-repetition, the inability to comprehend a reply due to the subject not being shown [makes it] a ground for defeat through the inability to respond alone; and because, apart from the occasion of showing the subject of the reply, repetition is pointless.

body.text: tathājñāne 'pyuttarāpratipattyaiva nigrahasthānatvam / ajānānaḥ kathamuttaram uttaraviṣayaṃ ca brūyāt? iti viṣayājñānamuttarājñānaṃ ca nigrahasthānam / anyathā evaṃ sati apratibhayā [? apratibhāyā] nirviṣayatvāt /
body.translated_text: Likewise, in the case of ignorance too, non-comprehension of the response itself constitutes the point of defeat. How could one who does not know state a response or the subject of a response? Thus, ignorance of the subject and ignorance of the response constitute the point of defeat.

body.text: anavadhāritārtho hi nānubhāṣate, ananubhāṣamāṇo viṣayamupadarśyottaraṃ pratipattuṃ na śaknuyādityuttaraṃ na pratipadyeta; jñātottaratadviṣayasyottarāpratipatterasambhavāt / ubhayametaduttarāpratipatteḥ kāraṇamiti /
body.translated_text: For one who has not ascertained the meaning does not respond; not responding, he would be unable to comprehend the response by indicating the subject — thus he would not comprehend the response. But for one who has known the response and its subject, non-comprehension of the response would not occur.

body.text: tadabhāve pratipattirbhavatyeveti tayoḥ pṛthagvacane 'pratibhāyāḥ ko viṣaya iti vaktavyam ! nirviṣayatvādavācyaiva syāt /
body.translated_text: In the absence of those [conditions], comprehension does occur — therefore, when they are stated separately, one must ask: what is the subject of non-apprehension (<s>apratibhā</s>)? Being without a subject, it would be simply unspeakable.

body.text: 80. nottarajñānam [? nottarājñānam] ajñānam / kiṃ tarhi? viṣayājñānam / jñāte hi viṣaye uttarājñānāt tanna pratipadyeteti asti viṣayo 'pratibhāyā iti cet / evaṃ tarhi ananubhāṣaṇaṃ nirviṣayam; ajñānenākṣepāt / na hi viṣayaṃ samyak pratipadyamānaḥ kaścinnānubhāṣeteti nānanubhāṣaṇaṃ pṛthag vācyam /
body.translated_text: 80. It is not ignorance of the response. What then? It is ignorance of the subject. For when the subject is known, one would not comprehend the response due to ignorance of the response — thus there is a subject of non-apprehension.

body.text: uttarājñānasya cākṣepāt / viṣayājñānenottarājñānamapyākṣiptameva na hi viṣayamajānannuttaraṃ jānātīti naivāpratibhāyā viṣayo 'sti /
body.translated_text: And because ignorance of the response is implied [by ignorance of the subject]. Ignorance of the response is already implied by ignorance of the subject — for one who does not know the subject does not know the response — therefore non-apprehension has no separate subject.

body.text: jñāte 'pi viṣaye punaruttarājñānamapratibhāyā viṣaya iti cet / evaṃ tarhi viṣayottarājñānayorapi prabhedāt nigrahasthānāntarālavācyāni [nigrahasthānāntarāṇi vācyāni?] / yathājñānasya viṣayo jñānam [? viṣayājñānam] uttarājñānamiti prabhedādasatyapi guṇātiśaye nigrahasthānāntaravyavasthā kriyate, tathājñānayorapi sarvottarājñānamityādi prabhedānnigrahasthānāntarāṇi kiṃ nocyante? na cobhayasyāpyajñānasya (

children.translated_text: [Reference marker: Vn 130]

children.text: ) saṃgrahavacane doṣaḥ, guṇastu lāghavasaṃjñaḥ syāditi saṃgrahavacanaṃ nyāyyam / tasmādananubhāṣaṇājñānayorapratibhāviṣayatvānna pṛthagvacanam /
children.translated_text: There is a fault in excessive enumeration, while the virtue of brevity is called economy — hence a comprehensive statement is proper. Therefore, since non-response and ignorance are the subjects of non-apprehension, a separate statement is not [needed].

body.translated_text: If it be said: even when the subject is known, ignorance of the response is the subject of non-apprehension — then, since there is a further division between ignorance of the subject and ignorance of the response, [yet more] separate points of defeat would need to be stated.

body.text: api ca - na pūrvottarapakṣavādino hetvābhāsāpratibhābhyāmanyat nigrahasthānaṃ nyāyyamasti, tadubhayavacanenaiva sarvamuktamiti / tadubhayākṣiseṣu prabhedeṣu guṇātiśayamantareṇa vacanādare 'tiprasaṅgāt vyarthaḥ prapañca iti /
body.translated_text: Moreover — for debaters of the prior and subsequent positions, there is no legitimate point of defeat other than fallacious reasons and non-apprehension. Everything is said by the statement of these two alone. In the remaining [points] subsumed under these two, the proliferation [of categories] —

body.text: 81. [16.] "uttarasyāpratipattirapratibhā /" [nyā.sū. 5.2.18] parapakṣapratiṣedhe uttaraṃ yadā na pratipadyate, tadā nigṛhīto vaktavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: 81. [16.] 'Non-comprehension of the response is non-apprehension.' [<s>Nyāya Sūtra</s> 5.2.18] When one does not comprehend the response to the refutation of the opponent's position, then he should be declared defeated.

body.text: sādhanavacanānantaraṃ prativiṣayamuttare vyarthaṃ tadajñānakramaghoṣaṇaślokapāṭhādinā kālaṃ gamayan kartavyāpratipattyā nigrahārha iti nyāyyaṃ nigrahasthānamiti /
body.translated_text: After the statement of proof, when one wastes time regarding the response to each point — through the recitation of verses proclaiming ignorance in sequence and so forth, while feigning non-comprehension of what should be done — he deserves censure. This is a legitimate point of defeat.

body.text: 82. [17.] "kāryavyāsaṅgāt kathāvicchedo vikṣepaḥ /" [nyā. sū. 5.2.20] yatkiñcit kartavyaṃ vyāsajya kathāṃ vicchinatti / 'idaṃ me karaṇīyaṃ prahīyate, asminnavasite paścāt kariṣyāmi / pratiśyākalāme kaṇṭhaṃ kṣiṇoti'; - ityevamādinā kathāṃ vicchinatti / sa vikṣepo nāma nigrahasthānamekataranigrahāntāyāṃ kathāyāṃ svayameva kathāntaṃ pratipadyate iti /
body.translated_text: 82. [17.] 'Interruption of the discussion by involvement in other business is distraction (<s>vikṣepa</s>).' [<s>Nyāya Sūtra</s> 5.2.20] One interrupts the discussion by engaging in any [other] business. 'This thing I must do is being neglected' —

body.text: idamapi yadi pūrvapakṣavādī kuryād vyājopakṣepamātreṇa, na punarbhūtasya tathāvidhakathoparodhinaḥ karyasya bhāve, tasya svasādhanāsāmarthyaparicchedādeva vikṣepaḥ syāt / tathā cedamarthāntaragamane evāntarbhavet; asamarthasādhanābhidhānāt (

children.translated_text: [Reference marker: Vn 133]

children.text: ) hetvābhāseṣu vā / prakṛtasādhanāsambaddhapratipatteśca nirarthakāpārthakābhyāṃ ca na bhidyate / atiprasaṅgaścaivamprakārāṇāmasambaddhasādhanavākyapratipattibhedānāṃ pṛthag nigrahasthānavyavasthāpane proktaḥ /
children.translated_text: — or among the fallacious reasons. And the comprehension of something unconnected with the proof at hand is not different from the meaningless and the purposeless. And there is an over-extension for unconnected proof-sentences of this kind —

body.translated_text: If the proponent does this merely as a pretextual interruption, but not when there is a genuine obstruction of that kind to the discussion — since his inability to prove his own thesis [would be evident] —

body.text: athottaravādī evaṃ vikṣipet, sādhanānantaram uttare pratipattavye tadapratipattyā vikṣepapratipattirapratibhāyāmarthāntare vāntarbhavati /
body.translated_text: If the respondent distracts in this manner, since the response must be comprehended after the proof, the non-comprehension of the response — [which constitutes] the apprehension of distraction — is subsumed under non-apprehension or under a different topic.

body.text: 83. nanu nāvaśyaṃ sādhanadūṣaṇābhyāmeva sarvasya pratipattiḥ, yena sarvā vādiprativādinorna samyak pratipatterhetvābhāse 'rthe pratibhāyāṃ vāntarbhavāt / bhavati hi anibaddhenāpi kathāprapañcena vivāda iti / na; asambhavāt / ekatrādhikaraṇe viruddhābhyupagamayorvivādaḥ syāt; aviruddhābhyupagamayoranabhyupagamayorvā virodhābhāvāt / tatrāvaśyamekasya vāgvacanapravṛttiḥ; yugapatpravṛttau parasparavacanagrahaṇāvadhāraṇottarāṇāmasambhavena pravṛttivaiphalyāt svasthātmanāmapravṛtteḥ / tena ca svopagamopanyāse 'vaśyaṃ sādhanaṃ vaktavyaṃ; anyathā pareṣāmaprattipatteḥ / apareṇa ca tatsambandhi dūṣaṇam / ubhayorasamyakpratipattau hetvābhāsāpratibhayoḥ prasaṅga iti sarvo nyāyapravṛttaḥ pūrvottarapakṣopanyāso dvayaṃ nātipatati /
body.translated_text: 83. But it is not the case that all comprehension arises only from proof and refutation, such that every instance of incorrect comprehension by proponent and respondent would be subsumed under fallacious reason, or under apprehension of a [different] meaning, or under non-apprehension —

body.text: etenaiva vitaṇḍā pratyuktā; abhyupagamābhāve vivādābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: By this very [argument], <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive debate) is also refuted — for in the absence of an accepted thesis, there is no dispute.

body.text: 84. yadā tarhyabhyupagamya vādaṃ viphalatayā na kiñcid vakti, anyadvā yatkiñcit pralapati, tadā kathaṃ hetvābhāsāntarbhāvaḥ?
body.translated_text: 84. When, however, having accepted the debate, one says nothing due to futility, or prattles something else or whatever — how then is it subsumed under fallacious reasons?

body.text: asamarthitasādhanābhidhāne evamuktam / anabhidhānānyābhidhānayorapi parājaya evetyuktam; abhyupagamya vādamasādhanāṅgavacanāt /
body.translated_text: This was stated regarding the statement of an unsupported proof. It has been said that even in the case of non-statement or other statement, there is defeat — because, having accepted the debate, one states what is not a component of proof.

body.text: etenādhikasya punaruktasya ca pratijñādervacanasya na nigrahasthānatvaṃ vyākhyātam / tadapi hi pratipāditārthaviparyayatvātsādhanasāmarthyavidhānamapratītapratyayatayā na lakṣaṇāt sādhanasya / asādhanāṅgavacanamiti nigrahasthānamiti /
body.translated_text: By this, it is explained that the statement of a thesis and the like that is excessive or repetitious is not a point of defeat. For that too, being the opposite of the established meaning, is an inappropriate application of proof-capacity —

body.text: 85 [18.] : "svapakṣadoṣābhyupagamāt parapakṣe doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā /" [nyā. sū. 5.2.21] yaḥ pareṇa coditaṃ doṣamanuddhṛtya bhavato 'pyayaṃ doṣa iti bravīti, yathā - 'bhavāṃścauraḥ puruṣatvāt'; ityukte sa taṃ prati brūyād- bhavānapīti / sa svapakṣe doṣābhyupagamāt parapakṣe taṃ doṣaṃ prasañjayan paramatamanujānātīti matānujñā nigrahasthānamiti /
body.translated_text: 85. [18.] 'The admission of a fault in one's own position and [the assertion of] the consequence of a fault in the opponent's position is concession of doctrine (<s>matānujñā</s>).' [<s>Nyāya Sūtra</s> 5.2.21] One who, without removing a fault charged by the opponent, [instead says] 'this fault applies to you too' —

body.text: atrāpi yadi puruṣatvāccauro bhavānapi syāt, na ca bhavatātmaivamiṣṭaḥ, tasmānnāyaṃ cauryaheturiti yadyayamabhiprāyaḥ, tadā na kaściddoṣaḥ, anabhimate tadātmani cauratvena hetudarśane dūṣaṇāt /
body.translated_text: Here too, if the intent is: 'because of being a person, you too could be a thief — but you yourself do not accept this — therefore this is not a reason for theft' — then there is no fault, since what is not accepted [is being used to show deviation].

body.text: prasaṅgamantareṇaivamṛjunaiva krameṇa kiṃ na vyabhicārita iti cet / yatkiñcidetat / santi hyevamprakārā api vyavahārā loka iti /
body.translated_text: If it be asked: why not simply show the deviation directly without employing the <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio) method? — this is of no consequence. For there are indeed such conventions in the world.

body.text: atha tadupakṣepamabhyupagacchati, etadapi uttarāpratipattyaiva tatsādhane nigrahārhaḥ / nāparatra; svadoṣopakṣepāt / tatsādhananirdoṣatāyāṃ hi tadabhyupagama evottarāpratipattiriti tāvataiva pūrvamāpannanigrahasya paradoṣopakṣepasyānapekṣaṇīyatvāditi /
body.translated_text: But if one accepts the opponent's charge — even then, one deserves defeat due to non-comprehension of the response in establishing that [counter-charge]. Not otherwise, because of introducing a fault in one's own position. For the acceptance of that [charge] depends on [one's failure to demonstrate] the faultlessness of one's own proof.

body.text: 86. [19.] "nigrahaprāptasyānigrahaḥ paryanuyojyopakṣaṇam /" [nyā.sū. 5.2.22]paryanuyojyo gāma nigrahopapattyā codanīyaḥ / tasyopekṣaṇaṃ nigrahaprāptau satyananuyogaḥ / etacca 'kasya parājayaḥ'; ityanuyuktayā parṣadā vaktavyaṃ, na khalu nigrahaprāptaḥ svakaupīnaṃ vivṛṇuyāditi /
body.translated_text: 86. [19.] 'The non-censure of one who deserves censure is the overlooking of the censurable (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>).' [<s>Nyāya Sūtra</s> 5.2.22] The censurable means one who should be challenged on the grounds that defeat is warranted. Overlooking him when defeat is warranted —

body.text: atrāpi yadi sādhanavādinaṃ nigrahaprāptamuttaravādī na paryanuyuṅkte, aprati- bhaivāsyottarāpratipatteriti na paryanuyojyopekṣaṇaṃ pṛthag nigrahasthānam / nyāyacintāyāṃ punarna dvayorekasyāpyatra jayaparajājayau; sādhanābhāsenārthāpratipādanāt, bhūtadoṣānabhidhānācca /
body.translated_text: Here too, if the respondent does not challenge the proponent when defeat is warranted — then his non-comprehension of the response is simply non-apprehension. Therefore, overlooking the censurable is not a separate point of defeat.

body.text: 87. atha kañciddoṣamudbhāvayati, kañcinna, na tadā nigrahamarhati; uttarapratipatteḥ /
body.translated_text: 87. But when he raises some faults and not others — then he does not deserve defeat, because the response has been comprehended.

body.text: arhatyeva, sato doṣasyānudbhāvanāditi cet / na santa iti kṛtvā sarve doṣā avaśyaṃ vaktavyāḥ /
body.translated_text: If it be said: he does deserve [defeat] because he has not raised an existing fault — not all faults must necessarily be stated on the grounds that they exist.

body.text: avacane vā nigrahaḥ; ekenāpi tatsādhanavighātādekasādhanavacanavat /
body.translated_text: Or, [there is] defeat in non-statement — because even one [fault] suffices to destroy the proof, just as the statement of even one proof [suffices].

body.text: yathaikasyārthasyānekasādhanasadbhāve 'pyekenaiva sādhanena tatsiddherna sarvopādānam iti na doṣamudbhāvayannevāparasyānudbhāvanānnigrahārhaḥ pūrvavat /
body.translated_text: Just as, even when multiple proofs for a single thesis exist, it is established by a single proof alone and not all need be employed—so one who merely exposes a fault is not defeated for not exposing another, as before.

body.text: atha pūrvapakṣavādī uttarapakṣavādinaṃ nigrahaprāptaṃ na nigṛṇhāti, tadā tayornyāye naikasyāpi pūrvavat jayaparājayau; doṣābhāsaṃ bruvāṇamuttaravādinaṃ svasādhanādanutsārayato 'samarthitasādhanatvānna jayo vādinaḥ; sarvadoṣāsambhavapradarśanena sādhanāṅgāsamarthanāt / nāpyuttaravādinaḥ, ubhayadoṣāpratipādanāt /
body.translated_text: Now, if the proponent does not defeat the respondent when the latter has arrived at the point of defeat, then in their debate neither achieves victory or defeat, as before. Since the respondent who states a pseudo-fault is not driven from his own proof, the proponent's proof remains unsubstantiated, so there is no victory for the proponent—because the members of the proof are not substantiated by demonstrating the impossibility of all faults. Nor is there [victory] for the respondent, because the faults of both sides are not demonstrated.

body.text: tasmādevamapi na paryanuyojyopekṣaṇaṃ nāma parājayādhikaraṇamiti /
body.translated_text: Therefore, even in this way, the 'neglect of what should be questioned' (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>) is not a ground of defeat.

body.text: 88. [20.] "anigrahasthāne nigrahasthānānuyogo niranuyojyānuyogaḥ /" [nyā. sū. 5.2.23] nigrahasthānalakṣaṇasya mithyāvyavasāyādanigrahasthāne nigṛhīto 'sīti paraṃ bruvan niranuyojyānuyogānnigṛhīto vaktavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: 88. [20.] 'Challenging [someone] at a point of defeat where there is no point of defeat is [the defeat called] questioning the unquestionable (<s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s>).' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.23] One who, through false determination of the definition of a point of defeat, says to the other 'you are defeated' where there is no point of defeat—he is to be declared defeated by the [fault of] questioning the unquestionable.

body.text: atrāpi yadi tatsādhanavādinamabhūtaistaddoṣairuttaravādyabhiyuñjīta, so 'sthāne nirdoṣe nigrahasthānasya niyoktodbhāvayitā na bhavati tathā / bhūtadoṣodbhāvanalakṣaṇasyottarasyā- pratipatteritareṇottarābhāsatve pratipādite 'pratibhayaiva nigṛhīta iti nedamato nigrahasthānāntaram /
body.translated_text: Here too, if the respondent challenges the proponent with non-existent faults, he is not a valid expositor of a point of defeat at a place that is faultless. And when the respondent's reply has the characteristic of exposing a genuine fault, if the other [proponent] demonstrates it to be a pseudo-reply, [the respondent] is defeated by [his own] lack of response—so this is not a separate point of defeat.

body.text: athottaravādinaṃ sādhanadoṣamudbhāvayantamaparo doṣābhāsavacanenābhiyuñjīta, tasya tena bhūtadoṣatve pratipādite sādhanābhāsavacanenaiva nigṛhīta iti /
body.translated_text: If another challenges the respondent who is exposing a fault of the proof, with the statement of a pseudo-fault, then when the genuine fault is demonstrated by the former, [the challenger] is defeated by the very statement of the proof-fallacy.

body.text: evamapi nedaṃ hetvābhāsebhyo bhidyate / avaśyaṃ hi viṣayāntaraprāptyarthaṃ hetvābhāsā nigrahasthānatvena vaktavyāḥ, taduktāvaparoktiranarthiketi /
body.translated_text: Thus this too does not differ from pseudo-reasons. For pseudo-reasons must necessarily be stated as points of defeat in order to reach other subject matters; their restatement [separately] is purposeless.

body.text: 89. [21.] "siddhāntamabhyupetyāniyamāt kathāprasaṅgo 'pasiddhāntaḥ /" [nyā. sū. 5.2.24] kasyacidarthasya tathābhāvaṃ pratijñāya pratijñātārthaviparyayāt kathāprasaṅgaṃ kurvato 'pasiddhānto vijñeyaḥ / tathā 'na sato vināśaḥ, nāsadutpadyate'; iti siddhāntamabhyupetya pakṣamavasthāpayati - 'ekāntā prakṛtiḥ vyaktasya avyaktalakṣaṇā; vikārāṇām anvayadarśanāt / mṛdanvayānāṃ śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭamekaprakṛtikatvam / tathā cāyaṃ vyaktabhedaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohasamanvito gṛhyate, tatsukhādibhirekaprakṛtiḥ'; iti /
body.translated_text: 89. [21.] 'When, after accepting a <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine), the discussion leads to an indefinite conclusion, [that is the defeat called] <s>apasiddhānta</s> (deviation from doctrine).' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.24] When one asserts the existence of a certain thing and then, through the reversal of the asserted meaning, creates an indefinite extension of the discussion—that should be known as <s>apasiddhānta</s>. For example, having accepted the doctrine 'There is no destruction of what exists; what does not exist does not arise,' one establishes the thesis: '<s>Prakṛti</s> is the sole source of the manifest; it has the character of the unmanifest; because of the observed continuity of modifications. Just as dishes etc. that are continuous with clay are observed to have a single source, so too this manifest world is apprehended as pervaded by pleasure, pain, and delusion; therefore through pleasure etc. it has a single source.'

body.text: sa evamuktavān paryanuyujyate - atha prakṛtirvikāra iti kathaṃ lakṣayitavyam? yasyāvasthitasya dharmāntaranivṛttau dharmāntaraṃ pravartate sā prakṛtiḥ, yat tad dharmāntaraṃ sa vikāra iti / so 'yaṃ prakṛtārthaviparyayādaniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayati / pratijñātaṃ cānena - 'nāsadāvirbhavati, na sat tirobhavati'; iti /
body.translated_text: Having stated thus, he is questioned: 'How then is <s>prakṛti</s> (source) to be distinguished from <s>vikāra</s> (modification)?' 'That which, while remaining stable, when one property ceases, another property arises—that is <s>prakṛti</s>; the other property that arises is <s>vikāra</s>.' This [proponent], through the reversal of the asserted meaning and the resulting indefiniteness, extends the discussion. For he has asserted: 'What does not exist does not come into being; what exists does not disappear.'

body.text: 90. sadasatośca tirobhāvāvirbhāvāvantaraṇa na kasyacit pravṛttyuparamaḥ, pravṛttirvā- ityevaṃ pratyavasthite yadi sa sata ātmahānamasataścātmalābhamabhyupaiti, apasiddhānto bhavati / atha nābhyupaiti, pakṣo 'sya na sidhyatīti /
body.translated_text: 90. And since there is no disappearance of what exists and no appearance of what does not exist, there is no cessation of activity nor any activity for anything whatsoever—when thus countered, if he accepts the loss of identity of what exists and the gain of identity of what does not exist, it is a deviation from doctrine (<s>apasiddhānta</s>). But if he does not accept [this], his thesis is not established.

body.text: ito 'pi na kaścidaniyamāt kathāprasaṅgo yattenopagataṃ nāsadutpadyate na sadvinaśyati'; iti tasya samarthanāyedamuktam 'ekaprakṛtikamidaṃ vyaktamanvayadarśanād'; iti / tatraikā prakṛtiḥ sukhaduḥkhamohāstadavibhaktayonikam idaṃ vyaktaṃ, tadanvayadarśanāt / vyaktasya tatsvabhāvatābhedopalabdheriti /
body.translated_text: Moreover, there is no indefinite extension of discussion from this [point], since what he has accepted—'what does not exist does not arise, what exists does not perish'—for the substantiation of that, this was stated: 'this manifest world has a single source, because of observed continuity.' Therein, the single source is pleasure, pain, and delusion; this manifest world has an undifferentiated origin in them, because of the observed continuity with them—because of the perception of the identity of nature of the manifest with them.

body.text: sukhādīnāmutpattivināśābhyupagamābhāvāt sarvasya tadātmakasya notpatti- vināśāviti siddhaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text: Since there is no acceptance of the arising and perishing of pleasure etc., there is no arising and perishing of anything that has their nature—thus [the thesis] is established.

body.text: 91. atra taduktasya hetordoṣamanudbhāvya vikāraprakṛtilakṣaṇaṃ pṛcchan svayamayaṃ prakṛtāsambandhena aniyamāt kathāṃ pravartayati / tatredaṃ syād vācyaṃ - vyaktaṃ nāma pravṛttinivṛttidharmakaṃ, na tathā sukhādayaḥ, vyaktasya sukhādyanvaye sukhādisvabhāvatā pravṛttinivṛttidharmatālakṣaṇamavahīyata iti / na tadrahitasukhādisvabhāvatā, vyaktalakṣaṇavirodhāditi, sukhādyanvayadarśanādityasiddho heturiti /
body.translated_text: 91. Here, without exposing the fault of the stated reason, the questioner himself, by asking about the definition of modification and source, extends the discussion to an indefinite [digression] through what is unconnected with the subject. Here this should be said: the manifest has the property of arising and ceasing; pleasure etc. are not like that. If pleasure etc. are continuous with the manifest, the manifest's nature as pleasure etc. would lose its characteristic of being subject to arising and ceasing. Therefore, the nature of pleasure etc. without [that characteristic] is contradictory to the definition of the manifest—hence the reason 'because of observed continuity with pleasure etc.' is unestablished.

body.text: evaṃ hi tasya sādhanadoṣodbhāvanena pakṣo dūṣito bhavati / so 'nupasaṃhṛtya sādhanadoṣaṃ, kathāṃ pratānayan svadoṣaṃ paratropakṣipati /
body.translated_text: For thus, by exposing the fault of his proof, his thesis is refuted. But instead, without concluding [by exposing] the fault of the proof, [the questioner] extends the discussion and transfers his own fault to the other side.

body.text: ayameva doṣo 'nena prakāreṇocyate iti cet /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] 'This very fault is stated in [the Nyāya] manner.'

body.text: eṣa naimittikānāṃ viṣayaḥ, na lokaḥ śabdairapratipāditamarthaṃ pratipattuṃ samartha iti, sa evāyaṃ bhaṇḍālekhyanyāyo 'trāpi /
body.translated_text: [Reply:] This is the domain of grammarians; ordinary people are not capable of understanding a meaning not expressed by words—and so the very same 'painting-the-pot analogy' [i.e., a mere labeling without substance] applies here too.

body.text: yathoktena nyāyena pūrvakasyāsādhanāṅgasyāsiddhasya hetorabhidhānādeva nigrahaḥ, nāpi niyamāt [aniyamāt?] kathāprasaṅgāt iti idamapi hetvābhāseṣvantarbhāvāt na pṛthagvācyam /
body.translated_text: By the reasoning already stated, defeat comes from the very statement of the unestablished reason that is not a valid member of proof; it does not come from the indefinite extension of discussion. Therefore, this too, being included within pseudo-reasons, need not be stated separately.

body.text: 92. [22.] "hetvābhāsāścayathoktāḥ /" [nyā.sū. 5.2.25] hetvābhāsāśca nitrahasthānāni / kiṃ punarlakṣaṇāntarayogād hetvābhāsā nigrahasthānatvamāpadyante, yathā pramāṇāni prameyatvam? ityata āha yathoktahetvābhāsalakṣaṇenaiva nigrahasthānabhāva iti /
body.translated_text: 92. [22.] 'Pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsas</s>) are as stated.' [<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.2.25] Pseudo-reasons are also points of defeat. The question arises: do pseudo-reasons acquire the status of points of defeat by possessing a separate definition, as means of valid cognition [acquire the status of] being knowable? To this [the sūtra] says: they are points of defeat by the very definition of pseudo-reasons as previously stated.

body.text: atrāpi yathoktatvāccintyemeva - kiṃ te yathā lakṣitaprabhedāstathaiva, āhosvidanyathaiveti? tattu cintyamānamihātiprasajyate iti na pratanyate / hetvābhāsāśca yathānyāyaṃ nigrahasthānamiti, etāvanmātramiṣṭamiti /
body.translated_text: Here too, since it says 'as stated,' this must be considered: are they exactly as defined and classified [earlier], or are they otherwise? But considering this would lead to over-extension here, so it is not elaborated. That pseudo-reasons are points of defeat according to proper reasoning—this much alone is accepted.

children.translated_text: 93. This <s>Vādanyāya</s>, which scrapes away the film of ignorance-darkness
for the vision of truth in the world, was composed by noble ones devoted to the welfare of others.
This ill-learned populace darkens that light of truth;
therefore effort has been made by me here for its re-illumination.

body.text:
vādanyāyo nāma prakaraṇaṃ samāptam /
[kṛtiriyamācāryadharmakīrticaraṇānām]
body.translated_text: The treatise named <s>Vādanyāya</s> is complete. [This is the work of the feet of the master <s>Dharmakīrti</s>.]
